No slides were found for this lecture. The page is built from the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Overview & risk factors

  • Cholelithiasis = gallstones in the gallbladder, symptomatic or not; ~70% are asymptomatic.
  • Symptomatic stones → biliary colic → if the pain is truly biliary → elective cholecystectomy. Confirm the symptoms are biliary first — removing the gallbladder won't fix unrelated pain.
  • Typical biliary colic: RUQ colicky pain → back ± right shoulder, often after a fatty meal.
  • Formation: rising bile cholesterol/salt concentration → precipitation → aggregation → stones.
Risk factors — "4 F": female, fatty (obesity), fertile (pregnancy/OCPs), forty + rapid weight loss.
  • Pain after a heavy meal in a woman with fatty-food episodes — the hormone responsible → cholecystokinin (CCK). 431
  • Gallstones are increased after bariatric surgery (rapid weight loss). 429 ×2
  • Prophylactic cholecystectomy is indicated for an enlarging gallbladder polyp > 1 cm. 441
  • Bile flow per day (keyed 500–1000 mL; the doctor quotes ~1–1.5 L/day; hepatic bile is watery, the gallbladder concentrates it). 426

Cholelithiasis vs acute cholecystitis

Biliary colic / cholelithiasisAcute cholecystitis
DefinitionStones, no inflammationWall inflammation, usually from stone obstruction
AnalgesiaImproves within ~4 hPain persists
Temperature / WBCNormalFever, raised WBC
US wallThin> 3 mm, oedematous, hyperaemic
Pericholecystic fluidAbsentPresent
  • Resistant biliary colic (pain persists but no fever, normal WBC, no wall thickening) is still surgical → expedited cholecystectomy.
  • Key sign of gallbladder inflammation → Murphy's sign 442 ×3; most sensitive and specific imaging for acute cholecystitis (keyed) → ultrasound. 434
  • RUQ colicky pain for 5 days + slight fever, not improving with fluids → acute cholecystitis 438; epigastric/hypochondrial pain, mild icterus, fever, leukocytosis → confirm with ultrasound. 439 ×11
  • Acalculous cholecystitis — the false statement → "CT is the investigation of choice" (US is first-line; it occurs in critically ill patients, 5–10% of cholecystitis, aggressive course). 426

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy — avoiding bile duct injury

  • Don't assume normal anatomy — duct variants are common (an aberrant right posterior hepatic duct can be mistaken for the cystic duct). Never clip or cut until the anatomy is clear. Retract via the gallbladder, not the liver.
Critical View of Safety: dissect the gallbladder neck and free the lower gallbladder from the liver bed until only two structures — cystic duct and cystic artery — enter the gallbladder. Then 2 clips on the retained side + 1 towards the gallbladder, and divide. The single key step to prevent major bile duct injury.
  • Intra-operative cholangiography = the "GPS" of the biliary tree when anatomy is unclear (inflammation, bleeding).
  • Complications: bile leak (cystic duct stump or accessory duct → biloma), bleeding (liver bed), major bile duct injury (rare, prevented by CVS).

Acute cholecystitis — timing

  • Inflamed gallbladder: thick, oedematous, friable (may need decompression to grasp); empyema = pus in the gallbladder.
  • Old: antibiotics, let it settle, delayed surgery weeks later. Now: early cholecystectomy in the same admission (RCTs: no more complications or conversions). If unsafe — call for help, convert or delay.
  • Acute cholecystitis (pericholecystic fluid, Murphy's) → cholecystectomy during the index admission. 442 ×4
  • RUQ pain for 8 days with fever (late presentation) → keyed delayed cholecystectomy in 2–3 months (beyond the early window). 435 ×4
  • 95-year-old, poor ASA, acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy. 441 ×4
  • Cholecystitis complicated by choledocholithiasis → ERCP + cholecystectomy. 438 ×2

How gallstones cause complications

  • Eating → CCK → gallbladder contracts → stones pushed to the cystic duct: a large stone impacts → cholecystitis; a small stone passes into the CBD → obstructive jaundice; impacts at the ampulla → biliary pancreatitis; CBD obstruction + infection → ascending cholangitis.
  • Mild gallstone pancreatitis → cholecystectomy in the same admission 442 ×11; gallstone pancreatitis with a dilated CBD → ERCP 442 ×2; initial management of gallstone pancreatitis → IV crystalloids. 438 ×3
  • Most common cause of acute pancreatitis → gallstones 441; obese woman with gallstones, continuous mid-abdominal pain, vomiting, epigastric tenderness → acute pancreatitis. 432 ×3
  • Severe pain 6 h after ERCP → post-ERCP pancreatitis. 442 ×3

Ascending cholangitis

  • Obstruction + infection → life-threatening. ERCP itself can cause cholangitis.
Charcot's triad: fever, RUQ pain, jaundice. Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension + altered mental status → severe, ICU.
  • Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, tachycardia, cholestatic LFTs → acute cholangitis 442 ×6; Charcot's triad → RUQ pain, fever and jaundice 429 ×4; the symptom in the list linked to the triad (jaundice) → keyed pruritus. 438 ×2
PatientManagement
Stable enough for endoscopyUrgent ERCP decompression (don't delay to tomorrow)
Severe infectionAvoid forceful contrast injection (pushes infected bile up)
Clearance unsafeStent first, stone later
Hypotensive / on inotropesPTC/PTBD under local (no sedation) → stabilise → ERCP → cholecystectomy
  • Cholangitis with 6 days of vomiting, T 39.6, dilated ducts → first IV fluids (then antibiotics and ERCP). 436 ×4

Obstructive jaundice — stone vs malignancy

  • Case: gallstones + dilated CBD, bilirubin 100 → ERCP to clear the CBD + cholecystectomy in the same admission. A CBD stent is only needed with cholangitis.
After ERCP clears a CBD stone, do the cholecystectomy in the same admission — don't discharge and wait months.
StoneMalignancy
OnsetAcuteGradual, weeks
PainPainful jaundicePainless jaundice
PatientYounger, often femaleOlder (60–70), weight loss, anorexia
CausesCholedocholithiasisPancreatic head, distal CBD cancer
  • Courvoisier sign: painless jaundice + palpable, non-tender gallbladder → distal malignant obstruction.
  • 67-year-old, painless jaundice, palpable gallbladder → carcinoma of the pancreatic head 438 ×9; Courvoisier → palpable gallbladder: jaundice unlikely from stones. 429 ×2
  • 70-year-old, progressive painless jaundice, obstructive LFTs → keyed ERCP 438 ×4; jaundice, itching, weight loss for 6 months → abdominal CT 429 ×2; US showing dilated intra- and extrahepatic ducts → investigation of choice keyed CT abdomen. 426
  • Obstructive jaundice, no fever, distended gallbladder, 2-cm CBD and intrahepatic dilatation (elderly) → CT with contrast (look for a malignant cause) 439; painless jaundice with a markedly dilated duct and intrahepatic dilatation in a 45-year-old → MRCP (define the anatomy — e.g. choledochal cyst). 439
  • Jaundice least adversely affects (keyed) → vision (pruritus/skin is affected). 426

ERCP, cholangiogram & choledochal cyst

  • ERCP — endoscopic, diagnostic and therapeutic (sphincterotomy, stone extraction, stent). MRCP — MRI, diagnostic only.
  • ERCP complications: pancreatitis (most common), bleeding (sphincterotomy), perforation (usually retroperitoneal), cholangitis. Reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis: pancreatic duct stent if repeated cannulation; aggressive LR hydration 24–48 h.
  • ERCP can't be done after gastrectomy (no access to the papilla). 426
  • Cholangiogram: a filling defect = stone. Normal CBD < 8 mm (~7 mm upper normal). Most CBD stones come from the gallbladder; primary duct stones form where bile stagnates.
  • Choledochal cyst: cystic dilatation of the CBD → stasis, stones, cholangiocarcinoma risk → resect the extrahepatic biliary tree + reconstruction (clearing stones isn't enough).
  • Stone extraction: balloon (first), basket/mechanical lithotripsy (large/hard stones), SpyGlass cholangioscopy (impacted stones).

Other biliary problems (from past exams)

  • Small-bowel obstruction with a rounded RIF opacity and air in the biliary tree → gallstone ileus 439 ×2; air in the biliary tree = pneumobilia. 427 ×2
  • Upper GI bleeding + jaundice with blood from the ampulla after a recent road traffic accident → cause trauma (haemobilia). 436

Biliary Tract

Jaundice
1. Overview
  • Definition: Jaundice refers to the yellow discoloration of the skin, sclera, and mucous membranes due to elevated serum bilirubin (>2.5 mg/dL).
  • Classification: Based on the site of dysfunction:
  • Prehepatic (Hemolytic) Jaundice: Excess bilirubin production due to hemolysis.
  • Hepatic (Hepatocellular) Jaundice: Impaired hepatic uptake, metabolism, or excretion of bilirubin.
  • Posthepatic (Obstructive) Jaundice: Blocked bile flow due to biliary obstruction.
2. Causes of Jaundice
TypeCommon Causes
Prehepatic (Hemolytic)Excess bilirubin production → Hemolysis (sickle cell, G6️PD
deficiency, autoimmune hemolysis), Gilbert’s syndrome,
Crigler-Najjar syndrome.
Hepatic (Hepatocellular)Liver dysfunction → Viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV), alcoholic liver disease, cirrhosis, drug-induced liver injury, primary biliary cholangitis, Wilson’s disease.
Posthepatic (Obstructive)Blocked bile outflow → Gallstones (choledocholithiasis),
malignancies (pancreatic, cholangiocarcinoma), biliary
strictures, sclerosing cholangitis, bile duct injury.
3. Clinical Presentation
Prehepatic (Hemolytic) Jaundice:
  • Pale stools & dark urine absent (bilirubin is unconjugated and not water- soluble).
  • Splenomegaly if hemolysis is chronic.
  • Increased reticulocyte count and low haptoglobin.
Hepatic (Hepatocellular) Jaundice:
  • Elevated transaminases (AST, ALT) → Liver cell injury.
  • History of viral hepatitis, alcohol use, drug toxicity.
  • Stools and urine normal or dark depending on conjugation status.
  • Ascites, spider angiomas, hepatomegaly in cirrhosis.
Posthepatic (Obstructive) Jaundice:
  • Pale (acholic) stools & dark urine (conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in urine).
  • Pruritus (bile salt accumulation).
  • RUQ pain, palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign) suggests malignancy.
4. Diagnostic Approach
A. Laboratory Tests
Serum Bilirubin:
  • Unconjugated (Indirect) bilirubin → Prehepatic causes.
  • Conjugated (Direct) bilirubin → Hepatic/posthepatic causes.
Liver Function Tests (LFTs):
  • AST/ALT → Hepatocellular injury (viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, ischemia).
  • Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) & γ-GGT → Cholestasis (biliary obstruction, primary biliary cholangitis).
  • Albumin & PT/INR → Liver synthetic function.
Other Tests:
  • Hemolysis markers: Reticulocyte count, LDH, haptoglobin (↓ in hemolysis).
  • Viral serology: HAV, HBV, HCV.
  • Autoimmune markers: ANA, AMA (primary biliary cholangitis), SMA (autoimmune hepatitis).
B. Imaging Studies
Ultrasound (First-line test for obstructive jaundice):
  • Ductal dilation → Extrahepatic obstruction.
  • Gallstones → Choledocholithiasis.
  • Mass or nodules → Suspect malignancy.
Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP):
  • Best non-invasive test for biliary obstruction & strictures.
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP):
  • Therapeutic & diagnostic → Used for stone extraction, stent placement.
Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS):
  • Better than CT for small bile duct & pancreatic tumors.
CT Abdomen with contrast:
  • Pancreatic & hepatic masses, lymphadenopathy, metastases.
Liver Biopsy (if needed):
  • Autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, Wilson’s disease.
5. Management Approach
A. Prehepatic (Hemolytic) Jaundice
Treatment depends on the cause:
  • Blood transfusions & folic acid (for hemolysis).
  • Avoid oxidative stress in G6PD deficiency.
  • Plasmapheresis in autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
B. Hepatic (Hepatocellular) Jaundice
Treatment is based on the underlying liver disease:
  • Acute viral hepatitis → Supportive care, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
  • Alcoholic hepatitis → Stop alcohol, nutritional support, corticosteroids if severe.
  • Autoimmune hepatitis → Steroids ± azathioprine.
  • Liver cirrhosis → Monitor for portal hypertension, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy.
  • Liver transplant if decompensated liver failure.
C. Posthepatic (Obstructive) Jaundice
Gallstones (Choledocholithiasis)
  • ERCP with stone removal.
  • Cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence.
Malignancy (Pancreatic, Cholangiocarcinoma, Periampullary Tumors)
  • Surgical resection if operable.
  • Palliative biliary stenting (ERCP) if unresectable.
  • Chemotherapy ± radiation for advanced cases.
Benign Biliary Strictures
  • Endoscopic balloon dilation & stenting.
Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)
  • Liver transplant in end-stage disease.
  • ERCP for strictures.
6. Prognosis & Follow-up
Depends on the underlying cause:
  • Acute viral hepatitis → Often self-limited, good prognosis.
  • Alcoholic liver disease → Progression depends on abstinence.
  • Liver cirrhosis → Requires long-term monitoring.
  • Obstructive jaundice (choledocholithiasis) → Excellent prognosis with ERCP.
  • Malignancies → Poor prognosis in advanced stages.
Follow-up includes:
  • LFT monitoring.
  • Tumor markers (CA 19-9 for pancreatic cancer).
  • Surveillance imaging (MRCP, ultrasound).
Diagnostic Examination of the Biliary Tree
1. Abdominal Ultrasound (US)
  • First-line imaging for suspected biliary disease due to high sensitivity and specificity.
  • Detects:
  • Cholelithiasis (Gallstones).
  • Cholecystitis (Gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign).
  • Bile duct dilation (suggests obstruction or choledocholithiasis). ✔ Limitations:
  • Misses small common bile duct (CBD) stones.
  • Sludge (calcium bilirubinate precipitate) may be seen but does not always indicate pathology.
2. Abdominal Computed Tomography (CT)
  • Used in unclear cases with abdominal pain, leukocytosis, and persistent jaundice.
  • Advantages:
  • Better than US for detecting pancreatic & distal bile duct pathology.
  • Detects masses, strictures, and pancreatitis.
  • Limitations:
    • Less sensitive than US for gallstones.
    • Cannot evaluate biliary function.
3. Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid (HIDA) Scan
  • Uses Tc-99m-labeled iminodiacetic acid (IDA) derivatives to evaluate bile flow.
  • Indications:
  • Acute cholecystitis (failure of gallbladder visualization within 30–60 min suggests cystic duct obstruction).
  • Biliary dyskinesia (calculates gallbladder ejection fraction after CCK stimulation).
  • Biliary leaks post-cholecystectomy.
  • Limitations:
    • Cannot directly visualize stones.
    • Lacks precision in localizing bile leaks.
4. Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
  • Non-invasive alternative to ERCP for bile duct imaging.
  • High sensitivity (~90%) and specificity (~90%).
  • Indications:
  • Suspected choledocholithiasis.
  • Biliary strictures, primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), or malignancies.
  • Limitations:
    • Does not allow therapeutic intervention.
5. Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
  • Gold standard for therapeutic intervention in bile duct pathology.
  • Indications:
  • Choledocholithiasis (stone removal).
  • Biliary obstruction (strictures, malignancy).
  • Sphincterotomy, stenting, or dilation.
  • Risks:
    • Post-ERCP pancreatitis, perforation, infection.
6. Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)
  • High-resolution imaging of the biliary tree, pancreas, and stomach.
  • Better than MRCP for detecting small CBD stones (89–94% sensitivity, 94– 95% specificity).
  • Advantages:
  • Can guide fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsies.
  • Immediate ERCP can be performed if needed.
7. Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC)
  • Used when ERCP fails or is not possible.
  • Indications:
  • Biliary strictures, cholangitis, or intrahepatic obstruction.
  • Malignancies blocking the bile ducts.
  • Limitations:
    • Invasive.
    • Risk of sepsis, bile leak, and hemorrhage.
8. Intraoperative Imaging
A. Intraoperative Cholangiogram (IOC)
  • Performed during laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy.
  • Indications:
  • Detects unsuspected CBD stones (2–10%).
  • Confirms biliary anatomy to avoid duct injury.
  • Limitations:
    • Requires fluoroscopy.
    • Cannot intervene if a stone is found.
B. Intraoperative Ultrasound (IOUS)
  • Provides high-resolution images of the biliary & vascular anatomy.
  • Highly sensitive for CBD stones.
  • Limitations:
  • Steep learning curve (~100 cases for mastery).
  • No real-time intervention.
9. Choosing the Best Test
IndicationBest Diagnostic Test
GallstonesUltrasound (first-line)
Acute CholecystitisUS → HIDA (if unclear)
CBD Stones (Choledocholithiasis)MRCP → ERCP (if intervention needed)
Biliary Obstruction (Mass/Stricture)MRCP, EUS, ERCP (if biopsy needed)
Biliary Leak (Post-Surgery)HIDA Scan

PSC, Cholangiocarcinoma

    • MRCP, ERCP, EUS + biopsy

Failed ERCP, Intrahepatic Obstruction PTC

Diseases of the Gallbladder
1. Gallstones & Biliary Colic
General Considerations
  • Present in ~30% of adults but symptomatic in only 20-25%.
  • Most gallstones contain cholesterol; others are pigmented stones (bilirubin-based).
  • Risk Factors: Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Family history. Also, rapid weight loss, pregnancy, and OCP use.
Clinical Features
  • Biliary colic (RUQ or epigastric pain, radiates to right scapula).
  • Postprandial pain (fatty meals), nausea, vomiting.
  • Murphy’s sign negative (distinguishes from acute cholecystitis).
Diagnosis
  • First-line: RUQ ultrasound (sensitivity: 95% for gallstones).
  • HIDA scan (for gallbladder function, dyskinesia).
  • CT scan (not first-line but can detect complications).
Treatment
  • Asymptomatic: No treatment unless high risk (large stones, porcelain gallbladder, gallbladder polyps >1 cm).
  • Symptomatic: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
  • Biliary Dyskinesia: Low gallbladder ejection fraction (<4️0%) → cholecystectomy.
2. Acute Cholecystitis
General Considerations
  • Gallstone impaction in cystic duct → inflammation.
  • Complications: Empyema, perforation, gallbladder gangrene, cholecystoenteric fistula.
Clinical Features
  • Persistent RUQ pain (>6 hours), fever, nausea, vomiting.
  • Murphy’s sign positive (inspiratory arrest on palpation).
  • Guarding and peritoneal signs (if perforation).
Diagnosis
  • First-line: RUQ ultrasound (gallstones, wall thickening >4 mm, pericholecystic fluid).
  • HIDA scan: Non-visualized gallbladder = cholecystitis.
  • Labs: Leukocytosis, mild LFT elevation, possible hyperbilirubinemia.
Treatment
  • Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 hrs) preferred.
  • Supportive: IV fluids, pain control, antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole).
  • High-risk patients: Percutaneous cholecystostomy if unfit for surgery.
3. Choledocholithiasis & Cholangitis
General Considerations
  • Choledocholithiasis: Stones in the common bile duct (CBD).
  • Cholangitis (Charcot’s triad): RUQ pain + fever + jaundice.
  • Reynolds’ pentad: + Hypotension & altered mental status → sepsis.
Diagnosis
  • Elevated ALP, GGT, bilirubin (direct).
  • Dilated CBD on ultrasound → Confirm with MRCP.
  • ERCP (gold standard) for both diagnosis & treatment.
Treatment
  • Stable: ERCP stone extraction.
  • Unstable: Emergency ERCP ± biliary drainage.
  • Supportive: IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole).
4. Gallstone Ileus
Pathophysiology
  • Cholecystoenteric fistula → large gallstone enters intestine → mechanical bowel obstruction (usually terminal ileum).
Diagnosis & Treatment
  • Imaging (Rigler’s Triad): Pneumobilia + SBO + ectopic gallstone.
  • Treatment: Enterotomy with stone removal ± cholecystectomy.
5. Biliary Tract Malignancy
Gastric Carcinoma
  • Strongest risk factor: H. pylori infection.
  • Early gastric cancer (superficial spreading): Good prognosis (5-year survival ~90%).
  • Diagnosis: Endoscopy with multiple biopsies.
  • Treatment: Surgical gastrectomy, neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Gallbladder Carcinoma
  • Risk Factors: Porcelain gallbladder, chronic cholecystitis.
  • Symptoms: Often late, mimic cholecystitis.
  • Diagnosis: CT scan, biopsy not always needed.
  • Treatment: Radical cholecystectomy.
Cholangiocarcinoma
  • Presentation: Painless jaundice, weight loss, pruritus.
  • Risk Factors: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), liver flukes.
  • Diagnosis: MRCP, ERCP with biopsy.
  • Treatment: Surgical resection if localized.
6. Jaundice Classification & Workup
Types of Jaundice
TypeCausesKey Labs
PrehepaticHemolysis (SCD, G6PD,↑ Unconjugated bilirubin,
(Hemolysis)spherocytosis)normal AST/ALT
Hepatic (Intrinsic liver disease)Hepatitis, Cirrhosis, Wilson’s↑ Both conjugated & unconjugated bilirubin, ↑AST/ALT
PosthepaticCholedocholithiasis,↑ Direct bilirubin, ↑ ALP,
(Obstructive)Cholangiocarcinoma, PSCdilated ducts on US
Workup

1. RUQ ultrasound (first-line for biliary obstruction).

2. CT/MRCP (for malignancy or unclear cause).

3. ERCP (if intervention needed).

Acalculous Cholecystitis, Emphysematous Cholecystitis, and Gallstone Ileus
1. Acalculous Cholecystitis
General Considerations
  • Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones.
  • Common in critically ill patients (trauma, TPN, sepsis).
  • Can lead to gangrene and perforation if untreated.
  • Pathogenesis: Ischemia, biliary stasis, bacterial infection (E. coli, Clostridium, Salmonella).
Clinical Features
  • Fever, leukocytosis, RUQ pain (often masked by critical illness).
  • No prior biliary colic history.
Diagnosis
  • RUQ ultrasound: Gallbladder distention, thickened walls, pericholecystic fluid.
  • HIDA scan: Non-visualized gallbladder.
  • CT scan: Shows inflammation and possible ischemia.
Treatment
  • IV fluids, antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole).
  • Urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy in unstable patients.
  • Cholecystectomy once stable.
2. Emphysematous Cholecystitis
General Considerations
  • Severe gallbladder infection caused by gas-forming bacteria (Clostridium, E. coli).
  • More common in men, diabetics.
  • Rapid progression to gangrene, perforation, sepsis.
Clinical Features
  • Sudden, severe RUQ pain, fever, leukocytosis.
  • More toxic appearance than typical acute cholecystitis.
  • Palpable RUQ mass in some cases.
Diagnosis
  • X-ray or CT: Air in the gallbladder wall (pneumobilia).
  • Ultrasound: Gas shadowing.
Treatment
  • Emergent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (pip-tazo or carbapenems).
  • Urgent cholecystectomy (if unstable, do percutaneous cholecystostomy first).
3. Gallstone Ileus
General Considerations
  • Mechanical small bowel obstruction due to a large gallstone (>2.5 cm).
  • Occurs in elderly women.
  • Pathophysiology: Cholecystoenteric fistula allows stone entry into the bowel → lodges in terminal ileum.
Clinical Features
  • Signs of small bowel obstruction: Crampy pain, distention, vomiting.
  • Intermittent symptoms as stone moves through the intestine.
  • Right upper quadrant mass possible.
Diagnosis
  • Abdominal X-ray/CT (Rigler’s Triad): 1. Pneumobilia (air in the biliary tree). 2. Small bowel obstruction. 3. Ectopic gallstone.
Treatment
  • Emergency laparotomy/laparoscopy → Enterotomy with stone removal.
  • Leave the gallbladder intact initially.
  • Elective cholecystectomy later if symptomatic.
Prognosis
  • High mortality (~20%) due to elderly comorbidities.
  • Early diagnosis & intervention improve survival.

Choledocholithiasis
1. Overview
  • Presence of stones in the common bile duct (CBD).
  • 15% of gallstone patients have CBD stones.
  • Can be asymptomatic or cause serious complications.
  • Two types: 1. Secondary stones (from gallbladder, most common). 2. Primary stones (form de novo in CBD, often pigment stones).
2. Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Biliary colic: RUQ/epigastric pain, radiates to scapula.
  • Jaundice: Fluctuating, intermittent.
  • Cholangitis (Charcot’s triad): Fever, RUQ pain, jaundice.
  • Pancreatitis: If obstruction affects pancreatic duct.
  • Pruritus: From prolonged jaundice.
Signs
  • Tender RUQ, possible hepatomegaly.
  • Icteric sclerae (if jaundiced).
  • Fever, tachycardia (if cholangitis).
3. Diagnosis
TestFindings
Labs↑ Bilirubin (mostly direct), ↑ ALP, mild ↑ AST/ALT,
leukocytosis in cholangitis
Ultrasound (1st line)Gallstones, CBD dilation (>6 mm)
MRCPNon-invasive, high sensitivity for stones
EUSHigh sensitivity for small stones
ERCPDiagnostic & therapeutic, gold standard
CT scanIdentifies dilated ducts/tumors
4. Differential Diagnosis
  • Cholangitis (if fever & chills present).
  • Biliary tumors (progressive jaundice without pain).
  • Hepatitis/cirrhosis (jaundice with systemic signs).
  • Pancreatitis (high lipase, amylase).
  • Primary biliary cholangitis (pruritus, fatigue, ↑ ALP).
5. Complications
  • Cholangitis (biliary infection, sepsis risk).
  • Hepatic abscess (from chronic infection).
  • Biliary pancreatitis (if pancreatic duct obstruction).
  • Biliary cirrhosis (from prolonged obstruction).
  • Gallstone ileus (rare, stone erodes into intestine).
6. Treatment

with CBD exploration

Cholangitis & Post-cholecystectomy Syndrome
1. Cholangitis (Bacterial Cholangitis)

Definition: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree due to biliary obstruction.

Causes:
  • Most common: Choledocholithiasis (CBD stones)
  • Others: Biliary strictures, tumors, chronic pancreatitis, ampullary stenosis, post-surgical complications (e.g., ERCP, biliary-enteric anastomosis).
Pathophysiology:
  • Biliary obstruction → Increased ductal pressure → Bacterial proliferation & systemic infection via hepatic sinusoids.

Complications:
  • Sepsis (bacteremia common).
  • Hepatic abscesses.
  • Secondary biliary cirrhosis (with chronic obstruction).
2. Post-cholecystectomy Syndrome (PCS)

Definition: Persistent or recurrent symptoms after gallbladder removal.

Causes:

1. Missed diagnosis: Original symptoms were not due to gallstones.

2. Residual biliary disease:

  • Retained CBD stones.
  • Biliary strictures.
  • Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD).

3. Other GI disorders:

  • Gastritis, GERD, IBS, pancreatitis.
Clinical Presentation:
  • Pain (episodic, postprandial RUQ or epigastric pain).
  • Dyspepsia, bloating, nausea.
  • Jaundice (suggests retained stone or stricture).
  • Cholangitis (if infection develops).
Diagnosis:
TestFindings
LFTs↑ Bilirubin, ALP (if bile duct obstruction)
MRCP/ERCPIdentifies strictures, stones, or Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction
EndoscopicConfirms SOD
Manometry

Biliary StrictureERCP with stenting

Gallbladder & Bile Duct Carcinomas
1. Carcinoma of the Gallbladder

Definition: Rare but aggressive malignancy, often associated with gallstones.

Risk Factors:
  • Gallstones (70% of cases) – Long-standing cholelithiasis increases risk.
  • Female gender – 2x more common in women.
  • Chronic inflammation – Porcelain gallbladder, chronic infections.
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis, carcinogen exposure.
Pathology:
  • Adenocarcinoma (most common - 85%).
  • Spreads early via direct invasion (liver, bile ducts, lymph nodes).
Clinical Features:
FeatureDescription
SymptomsRUQ pain (persistent, colicky), anorexia, weight loss.
JaundiceOccurs if tumor invades the bile duct.
Palpable massSuggests advanced disease.
CholangitisOccasional due to biliary obstruction.
Diagnosis:
TestFindings
Ultrasound / CTMass in gallbladder, liver invasion, biliary dilation.
MRCP / ERCPDefines extent of bile duct involvement.
CA 19-9, CEAMay be elevated, but non-specific.
HistologyConfirmatory if obtained preoperatively or incidentally after cholecystectomy.
Management:
StageTreatment
LocalizedRadical cholecystectomy + wedge liver resection
+ lymphadenectomy.
Incidental finding post- cholecystectomyReoperation for liver resection & lymphadenectomy if invasive.
UnresectablePalliative care: Stenting (biliary drainage),
chemotherapy (gemcitabine-based).
Prognosis:
  • 5-year survival: 10% (except incidental tumors detected early).
  • Most patients die within 1 year due to rapid spread.
2. Malignant Bile Duct Tumors (Cholangiocarcinoma)
Definition: Adenocarcinoma arising from the bile ducts, classified by location:
  • Perihilar (Klatskin tumor) – 60%.
  • Distal CBD – 20%.
  • Intrahepatic – 10%.
Risk Factors:
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
  • Congenital biliary cysts
  • Liver fluke infection (Asia)
  • Chronic biliary inflammation

FeatureDescription
Painless obstructive jaundiceMost common presentation.
PruritusDue to bile salt accumulation.
Dark urine, pale stoolsDue to bilirubin retention.
Anorexia, weight lossOccurs later.
Palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier’s sign)If distal CBD is involved.

TestFindings

Ultrasound / CTBiliary duct dilation, mass identification.

ERCP with biopsyConfirms diagnosis, allows for stenting.
CA 19-9Elevated in many cases, but non-specific.

  • Advanced disease survival: <1 year.
Benign Gallbladder & Biliary Tract Conditions
1. Benign Tumors & Pseudotumor of the Gallbladder

Definition: Non-malignant growths or lesions appearing as wall projections on imaging. Cancer should be suspected if the lesion is >1 cm.

Types of Gallbladder Polyps
TypeFeatures
Cholesterol PolypsMost common (non-neoplastic), lipid-laden macrophages,
may cause biliary colic.
Inflammatory PolypsRare, occur with chronic cholecystitis.
AdenomyomatosisThickened gallbladder wall, fundal involvement, possibly
congenital or degenerative.
AdenomasTrue neoplasms, may be associated with carcinoma in situ.
Management of Polyps
  • Cholecystectomy if:
  • Polyp >1 cm (malignancy risk).
  • Concerning imaging features (rapid growth, irregular shape).
  • Symptoms (biliary colic, pain).
  • Follow-up with serial ultrasound if <1 cm and asymptomatic.
2. Benign Bile Duct Tumors
  • Ductal Papillomas & Adenomas – Rare, often multiple, high recurrence risk.
  • Treatment: Complete surgical excision for cure.

Uncommon Causes of Bile Duct Obstruction
1. Congenital Causes
Choledochal Cysts
  • Features: Cystic dilation of bile ducts, presenting with jaundice, cholangitis, and RUQ mass.
  • Diagnosis: ERCP / MRCP / THC.
  • Treatment: Surgical excision + Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (high malignancy risk).
Caroli Disease
  • Features: Congenital intrahepatic bile duct dilation, associated with hepatic fibrosis & medullary sponge kidney.
  • Presentation: Cholangitis, jaundice, portal hypertension.
  • Treatment: Lobectomy (if localized), antibiotics for cholangitis.
2. Vascular & Trauma-Related
Hemobilia (Bleeding into Biliary System)
  • Causes: Trauma, tumors, hepatic artery aneurysm, parasitic infection.
  • Triad: RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding.
  • Diagnosis: Angiography, Tc-99m RBC scan.
  • Treatment: Angioembolization, surgical ligation if needed.
3. Pancreatic-Related Obstruction
Pancreatitis
  • Causes of Biliary Obstruction:
  • Acute: Swelling & inflammation of pancreas.
  • Chronic: Scar tissue & fibrosis compressing bile duct.
  • Pseudocyst: Direct compression.
  • Diagnosis: ERCP / MRCP.
  • Treatment:
  • Biliary drainage (choledochoduodenostomy) for chronic cases.
  • Pseudocyst drainage if obstructing bile flow.
4. Ampullary Dysfunction & Stenosis
  • Causes: Idiopathic, post-gallstone trauma, Sphincter of Oddi Dysfunction (SOD).
  • Symptoms: RUQ pain, jaundice, abnormal LFTs.
  • Diagnosis: ERCP + manometry, DISIDA scan.
  • Treatment: Endoscopic sphincterotomy for confirmed cases.
5. Structural & Infectious Causes
Duodenal Diverticula
  • Location: Near bile duct opening, can compress or distort the duct.
  • Treatment: Choledochojejunostomy or choledochoduodenostomy.
Ascariasis (Parasitic Infection)
  • Cause: Ascaris lumbricoides invasion into bile duct.
  • Symptoms: Biliary colic, jaundice, cholangitis.
  • Treatment: Anthelmintic drugs (mebendazole/albendazole), ERCP for worm removal.
6. Chronic Recurrent Cholangitis
Recurrent Pyogenic Cholangitis
  • Common in: Southeast Asia, associated with E. coli infections.
  • Findings: Intrahepatic pigmented stones, recurrent cholangitis, liver abscesses.
  • Diagnosis: ERCP / MRCP / THC.
  • Treatment:
  • Cholecystectomy + duct exploration.
  • Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy for strictures.
  • Lobectomy if disease is localized.
Sclerosing Cholangitis
  • Unknown cause, linked to ulcerative colitis (60%).
  • Symptoms: Jaundice, pruritus, cholestatic LFTs.
  • Complications: Bile duct strictures, cirrhosis, cholangiocarcinoma.
  • Diagnosis: MRCP/ERCP (beaded bile ducts).
  • Treatment:
  • Ursodiol for symptom relief.
  • Percutaneous balloon dilation for strictures.
  • Liver transplant for advanced cases.
